sources.entry: Volt - Open-source AI code editor built on VS Code (Code - OSS) that runs Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Kimi over ACP, with hunk-level keep/undo of agent edits.

summary.one_liner: Volt is an open-source, MIT-licensed code editor built on the VS Code core that puts coding-agent chat, code, Git, an in-app browser and a terminal in one window.
summary.what_it_does: Volt is a desktop editor built on the real VS Code core, so VS Code extensions, themes, keybindings, language servers and debuggers carry over. It adds an agent window with chat, a composer with several modes (Agent, Plan, Ask, Debug, Multitask), and a runtime that drives agent CLIs such as Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Kimi over ACP, as well as direct API providers and local models like Ollama and LM Studio. Agent edits stay pending until the user keeps or undoes them hunk by hunk, and each turn is checkpointed in Git under a hidden ref. Access presets control what an agent may read, edit, run or fetch. The workspace also includes an in-app browser the agent can drive, built-in Git (branches, worktrees, stashes, pull requests), and a terminal. The README describes it as a public beta below version 1.0.
use_cases: Work with Claude Code or Codex inside an editor
Review and selectively keep or undo AI agent edits
Run a local model through Ollama or LM Studio for coding
Give parallel agents separate Git worktrees
Drive and annotate a browser from a coding chat
Use VS Code extensions alongside an AI agent
notable: Built on the upstream VS Code core, so the extension ecosystem carries over
Hunk-by-hunk keep or undo of agent edits against a baseline
Per-turn Git checkpoints stored under refs/volt/* without touching the user's index
Four access presets plus a hard-deny list for destructive commands and secret files
Bring-your-own agent: uses existing agent CLI sign-ins or API keys and stores no provider credentials itself
caveats: Public beta below 1.0; expect rough edges and changes between releases
macOS is the primary tested platform; Windows and Linux have had little testing
Windows installers are not code-signed yet, so SmartScreen warns on install
Permissions are an approval policy, not a sandbox; allowed shell commands run as the user
